Native-L2 assets and L1 representations: the May 2023 bridge
baseline
Research date: 29 September 2026. Scope: conditional architecture and historical source review,
supported by read-only observations of inherited contract state. This note assumes the hypothetical
source rollup and its source execution state are supplied. The absence of a public pARB RPC is a
limitation on verifying history, not a reason to stop evaluating that architecture.
Architectural finding
The native-L2 lock/L1 mint mechanism was available before the PulseChain fork. Arbitrum's reverse
gateways preserve native tokens in L2 escrow and issue an authorized representation on L1. L1 escrow
of the represented underlying is not required for this model. ARB is a concrete integration of that
architecture whose L1 gateway, token and registration existed in the inherited snapshot.
The model is distinct from the ordinary return of an L1-origin asset. In that model, an L2 representation
is burned and existing L1 escrow is released. The same messaging system can support different asset-
accounting models because the destination gateway and token determine the accounting operation. An
accepted message does not itself decide whether a token is minted or transferred.
For the wider thesis, a transferable source vault receipt can be the asset held in escrow. Its underlying
may remain invested in the source protocol. This establishes conditional architectural plausibility for a
representation backed by locked source receipts. It does not establish that every existing L1 stablecoin
or vault receipt recognizes that representation as its own token.
pDAI stabilization thesis · 4 October 2026 86

Historical cut and evidence
The source cutoff is 10 May 2023, 22:36:11 UTC, corresponding to inherited Ethereum block 
17,232,999. The block returned by the public PulseChain RPC has hash 
0xe5667f9cafb115b1dcfc36b0b569a5601f01dfa000698140a1298ef4f87e2e37. Reads in this note use that inherited block
or explicitly identified earlier event blocks. They do not substitute 2026 state for the May 2023 baseline.
Repository commit queries were bounded by that precise cutoff:

Source availability at a date is not proof that every repository contract was deployed at that date.
Deployed ARB facts below therefore use historical state and receipts as well as published source. The
Optimism comparison deliberately uses the legacy packages/contracts bridge, not Bedrock code that was
also present in the contemporaneous repository.
The two Arbitrum accounting models
Asset origin and
direction
Source operation Destination operation Where backing remains
Ordinary L1-origin token, L1
→ L2
Transfer L1 token into
gateway escrow
Mint L2 representation L1 gateway
Ordinary L1-origin token, L2
→ L1
Burn L2 representation Transfer existing L1 token
from escrow
Escrow decreases as the
claim is retired
Native-L2 token, L2 → L1
through reverse gateway
Transfer L2 token into
gateway escrow
Mint authorized L1
representation
L2 gateway
Native-L2 representation
returning L1 → L2
Burn L1 representation Transfer native token out of
L2 escrow
Source escrow decreases as
the representation is retired
In the historical L1 base gateway, the ordinary incoming escrow operation transfers the L1 token to its
recipient. The L1 reverse override instead invokes the destination token's bridgeMint; its return operation
invokes bridgeBurn. The L2 reverse override transfers source tokens into custody and measures the
balance actually received. For the return, it transfers tokens out of custody. These function bodies
establish the direction despite an inconsistent direction comment in the historical source headers.
For a fixed-supply, non-rebasing source asset, let S be source token supply, E the amount locked for this
representation, and D the outstanding destination representation in equivalent units. At a settled
checkpoint in the simple one-to-one model, with no pending claims, D = E. Source circulating units are S −
E; adding destination units produces (S − E) + D = S. A destination mint increases that chain's token
pDAI stabilization thesis · 4 October 2026 87

supply while the source lock removes the matching amount from independent circulation. Adding the full
token supplies on both chains would count escrowed source tokens twice. Multiple destinations require
the total claims against an escrow allocation to be reconciled together.
During asynchronous transfers, committed escrow also covers pending issuance rights and pending
return rights. In a lossless fixed-unit model without donations, fees or unrelated allocations, E = D + I + R,
where I and R are those exclusive pending claims. Count each claim once as its processing status
changes. This is a conservation model, not a claim that all these terms are exposed by existing contract
getters. It explains why escrow and circulating representations need not be equal while a lock/mint or
burn/release is in flight.
This is representation backed by custody, rather than new independent source collateral. The identity
and redemption rights of the represented source token remain essential: custody of one receipt does not
make it redeemable as any other receipt or as an external dollar.
ARB was integrated before the fork
The reverse gateway 0xbbce8aa77782f13d4202a230d978f361b011db27 was created in transaction 0x1070…ee25, block
16,840,302, 16 March 2023, 12:07:11 UTC. Its successful receipt identifies the gateway as the newly
created contract and records implementation 0x4e8c24617c4592895d52ac6df29d9647e9d01bb5.
At block 16,840,312, 12:09:11 UTC that day, transaction 0x5cc8…6dae records registration connecting L1
ARB 0xb50721bcf8d664c30412cfbc6cf7a15145234ad1 with L2 ARB 0x912ce59144191c1204e64559fe8253a0e49e6548. These
are inherited Ethereum events, not new PulseChain governance actions.
At inherited block 17,232,999, both token and gateway have bytecode, the router's ARB mapping selects
this gateway, the token's arbOneGateway() returns this gateway, and the gateway's implementation is still 
0x4e8c…1bb5. Its verified implementation is L1ForceOnlyReverseCustomGateway. The historical force-only source
disables the ordinary token self-registration entry point. This is a governed/registered integration, not an
open mint facility for every fungible token.
The pre-cutoff L1 ARB token explicitly restricts bridgeMint and bridgeBurn to arbOneGateway. Its L2 counterpart
is a distinct source-chain contract. The later recorded PulseChain ARB mint in the companion bridge
observations (Appendix 5) therefore uses a destination capability already present in the inherited
architecture. That later mint does not establish the actual source collateral position; this historical
section establishes when the integration existed.
Which token classes fit the native-L2 custody model?
The relevant distinction is transferable units and their accounting behavior, not whether the token is
called a stablecoin, governance token or staking receipt.
Source class Architectural assessment
Ordinary transferable ERC-20 / PRC-20 Fits the balance/allowance/transfer custody interface.
Destination mint authority is a separate requirement.
Transferable ERC-4626 shares Fits as shares. The represented property is a claim on
source vault shares, whose source assets can remain
invested.
Static Aave receipt wrappers, cT okens and conventional
transferable vault shares
Often fit as fixed share units, subject to their actual
implementation. Redemption follows the source receipt's
rules.
pDAI stabilization thesis · 4 October 2026 88

Source class Architectural assessment
Rebasing receipts, including direct aT okens or OUSD-style
balances
Transferability alone is insufficient to specify the claim. A
fixed destination amount does not automatically track later
source rebases or interest.
Fee-on-transfer assets The reviewed source gateway measures actual received
amount. That does not alone account for fees on eventual
release or unrelated balance changes.
Nontransferable vault shares or debt positions Do not fit ordinary escrow transfer semantics merely
because they expose balance-like information.
ERC-721 / ERC-1155 Require NFT or multi-token custody and representation
semantics; the reviewed ERC-20 reverse gateway does not
supply those interfaces.
Native currency Requires its native-currency bridge model, or a separately
wrapped fungible token.
The relevant vault standard is ERC-4626, not an identified “4621” bridge category. ERC-4626 shares
implement ERC-20, but the standard permits nontransferable implementations to revert transfers.
“PRC-20” does not itself add remote mint permissions to the ERC-20 interface.
A static source wrapper can express interest as an increasing source conversion rate while the bridged
share count stays fixed. A rebasing receipt can change the escrow's token-unit balance after deposit.
These are different claim models. The generic reverse gateway does not by itself reconcile every
possible rate, fee, rounding convention or rebase across two separately executing protocols.
Exact existing pool coins and application permissions
Three identities must remain separate: a native source receipt, a destination representation of that
receipt, and an existing destination protocol's receipt. A new destination representation of source aDAI
may be backed by source aDAI without being the aDAI contract already accepted by a destination
Balancer wrapper. Equal symbols, equal decimal counts and matching numerical addresses on different
chains do not establish that relationship.
The necessary architecture has three separate permission layers:
Messaging recognizes the source message and counterpart contract.
The gateway recognizes the token pair and representation rule.
The exact destination token authorizes its issuer, and the downstream pool accepts that exact token
address.
ARB has explicit token-level bridge mint/burn support. An ordinary ERC-4626 mint operation instead
receives the vault's underlying asset to issue vault shares; the method name does not mean arbitrary
bridge issuance. Aave Portal is a further, application-specific destination issuance mechanism with its
own bridge role, reserve accounting and settlement rules. Generic reverse bridging does not
automatically satisfy Portal settlement or issue an existing Aave aT oken. Under assumed application
integration, these can be conditional routes; they should not be conflated with the unmodified generic
gateway behavior.
With source execution and the relevant token integration stipulated, it is architecturally coherent for
invested source receipts to remain locked while their exact authorized destination representation is
traded. That conditional statement is the positive result. It does not need a public source RPC to be
logically evaluated. Which integrations were actually deployed, and which specific source deposits
occurred, remain separate historical questions.

2. 
3. 
pDAI stabilization thesis · 4 October 2026 89

Validator control, source backing and registration
The audit does not establish abandonment of a pARB execution network or exclusive validator control by
the examined wallets. For conditional analysis these can be assumptions. The absence of a public source
endpoint is not itself proof of either claim.
Optimistic confirmation and genuine source execution are different evidence. Without an effective
honest challenger, the security premise that invalid claims are contested is lost. Acceptance by the
parent contracts is consequently not independent proof that the claimed source collateral exists. Nor
does a validator role automatically grant token/application administration. An assumed source
environment with actual, usable balances and correctly configured native applications is a stronger
premise than an accepted assertion alone.
Even granting that stronger premise, L1 contract behavior remains separate. An authenticated message
cannot by itself change a token's mint permission, turn a standard transfer into issuance, or make one
token address equivalent to another pool coin. A mintable reverse representation requires its destination
issuance path; an ordinary return requires transferable destination inventory. The ARB implementation
provides a concrete example of pre-existing authorized issuance, not a universal stablecoin issuer.
A formal new registration transaction is not universally necessary. Integrations can be inherited,
registration can be supplied by a bridge administrator or factory, and standard routes can use
predefined counterpart derivation. Which checks apply must be read from the actual entry point rather
than inferred from the presence of a function named register. This distinction does not remove the exact
destination token's transfer or issuance rules. Likewise, storing a token mapping is not itself a grant of
mint authority by that token.
Source reserve solvency in copied-token units can be stipulated consistently. It does not establish
external-dollar backing, automatic acceptance by L1 Aave or Curve, or separate backing for multiple
claims that reuse one collateral allocation. An L1 bridge can create a new representation without the
original issuer managing it, where the bridge design supports this; existing L1 pools still need to accept
that representation's exact address.
The main paper's source-state-control section applies these distinctions to ARB, ordinary escrow release,
factory-created representations, Aave Portal, OUSD/eUSD/mUSD and funded Across delivery. This is a
source/accounting review; no new state-changing experiments or public transactions were performed.
Legacy Optimism as a comparison
The May 2023 legacy L2 StandardBridge burns the L2 representation on withdrawal and identifies its
paired L1 token. The corresponding L1 StandardBridge authenticates the counterpart messenger,
reduces the recorded deposit amount for the token pair, and transfers existing L1 tokens to the recipient.
That standard return is not the Arbitrum native-L2 reverse model. A valid withdrawal message does not
make the legacy Optimism L1 standard bridge mint an arbitrary existing L1 token when its
corresponding escrow/deposit accounting cannot support the withdrawal. The existence of more general
cross-domain messaging does not change the standard bridge's programmed token operation. This
comparison concerns the reviewed legacy standard contracts, not every custom bridge or later Optimism
version.
What an L1 fork preserves
Copying Ethereum state preserves the L1 contracts, storage, token mappings, escrows and recorded
rollup commitments at the snapshot. It does not copy the separate L2 execution database simply
because an L1 contract contains its root or counterpart address. These are different layers of the system.
pDAI stabilization thesis · 4 October 2026 90

For this theoretical exercise, source-chain execution, balances and operating protocols may be explicit
assumptions. Under those assumptions, the analysis can assess token custody, authorization,
representation and redemption without requiring a public source endpoint. A historical assertion that a
particular source deposit occurred would require additional source or message evidence. Keeping those
claim types separate allows positive architectural findings without presenting assumptions as observed
transactions.
Reproduction record
The new batch is artifacts/parb-historical-bridge-models-20260929/. It contains the cutoff commit queries,
source manifest and source caches, inherited-block metadata/code/getter responses, bounded gateway
logs, and the deployment and registration receipts/blocks. Historical gateway log coverage is block
16,600,000 through 17,232,999. The selected deployment receipt directly reports the gateway's creation
address; its date is not inferred merely from the first log returned by that bounded query.
RPC observations use eth_getCode, eth_getStorageAt, getter eth_call, eth_getLogs, eth_getBlockByNumber and 
eth_getTransactionReceipt against https://rpc.pulsechain.com. They are one-provider observations. No
transaction payloads, privileged state changes or simulations were produced. Raw data and source
copies remain in ignored artifacts rather than this maintained study.
pDAI stabilization thesis · 4 October 2026 91
